title: Five Things I Learned about Sequence Design with Kris Boulton
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton stands in for a missing podcast guest and asks Kris Boulton to rebuild a novice teacher's volume-of-a-prism teaching sequence. Barton rates the original as strong, with controlled variation and a general rule, then draws out five changes Boulton made that transfer to any topic. Open with the general case rather than the special case, and keep arithmetic out until the concept is secure. Give more numbers than the task needs so that pupils must choose, and then remove the rule from the slide so it has to be retrieved. Finally, make intimidating numbers safe by removing the computation. Barton ends by confessing he would have used four teacher examples where Boulton used two, and argues for building the leanest sequence first and letting pupils' responses show where to add steps.
points: Introduce a rule with the version that shows it most cleanly, and save the special case, such as the cuboid, for the end.
Separate the concept from the arithmetic: build the expression first, then easy numbers, then awkward ones, so a wrong answer is diagnostic.
Supplying redundant measurements and distractors forces pupils to decide what is relevant, and reveals who is merely multiplying visible numbers.
Whatever stays permanently on display becomes a crutch, so state the rule memorably and then take it away and cold-call for it.
Design the leanest sequence you believe will work and field-test it, since over-atomising wastes time and pupil responses show where to break it down.
quotes: The lesson here is straightforward, but counter-intuitive: whenever you introduce a rule, reach for the version that shows the rule cleanly, not the special case that hides it or comes with its own exceptions, even though the special case may appear simpler. Save the special case for the end, when students can appreciate exactly what makes it different.
The idea you are teaching is that volume is an area multiplied by a perpendicular length. Working out that 12 × 5 = 60 is a separate skill.

His line for it was that you do not learn to ride a bike in the middle of the Tour de France. Of course, we want students fluent in arithmetic. Just not while they are also trying to work out what volume is.

The problem is that if every diagram hands you exactly two numbers, the task is no longer “work out the volume”. It is “find the two numbers and multiply them”. Students are no longer thinking about the concept of volume.

The general point is simple. Anything you leave permanently on display, students will use as a crutch rather than remember. If you want it in their heads, state it clearly, make it memorable, then take it away and make them retrieve it.

Fractions, surds, algebraic expressions, big numbers: students tend to fall apart at the sight of them. But the fear comes almost entirely from the computation they imply. Take the computation away, and a surd is just a label.
Design the leanest sequence you genuinely think will work, put it in front of students, and let their responses decide where it needs more steps. Not the other way round.
